A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison despite reformatting and an added appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation-similarity, centroid-ablation, norm-decomposition and probing results for DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2-7b and Gemma3-12b, including appendix experiments.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds Pythia-6.9b training-checkpoint results in Appendix H, Figures 11–12.

M1.justification: Centroid construction and projection ablation remain unchanged. However, the new checkpoint analysis orthogonalizes semantic centroids against syntactic centroids, reversing the order used in the retained Appendix G decomposition. This is a limited procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same generated English syntax twins, paraphrases and translations into Arabic, Chinese, German, Italian, Spanish and Turkish. Pythia checkpoints and token-count checks change model configurations or evaluation settings, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v4 Section 2.2 newly reports an informal comparison with last-token sentence representations, finding similar patterns but weaker signals than averaging or concatenation. The original no-ablation and randomly mismatched-centroid controls remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds a longitudinal evaluation of Pythia-6.9b at six checkpoints, from initialization to step 143000, measuring both layerwise norm decomposition and maxima across layers. It also reports six-token semantic-subset checks and recall@1/@2 evaluations. Corrections to published metric and centering formulas do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix H investigates when syntactic and semantic components emerge during training, extending the analysis beyond depth profiles of trained models. v4 also adds sensitivity findings for last-token aggregation, six-token semantic representations and retrieval cutoffs; the earlier ablations and controls are retained.

E5.justification: Existing similarity plots retain one-standard-deviation bands from five half-sample subsamplings, and Tables 3–4 remain explicitly single-run without variance estimates. The new checkpoint plot also uses standard-deviation shading but does not document a new estimation procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: Figures 11–12 add training-time findings absent from v1: syntax explains roughly half the squared norm around checkpoint 512, while semantic contributions develop later in central layers. Additional qualitative robustness findings are reported. All matched earlier plotted curves and Tables 3–4 retain their values; these are added results, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: v4 corrects Eq. (2)'s normalization from 1/N to 1/N_s^2, changes the nearest-neighbor condition in Eq. (3) from rank 0 to rank 1, and replaces Eq. (6)'s unsquared dot products with properly normalized squared projections. These repair existing mathematical definitions without introducing a new theoretical framework.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and principal conclusions retain the same claims: partial linear encoding, concentration of semantic information in inner layers, and asymmetric separability of syntax and semantics. The checkpoint evidence supports these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v4 interprets training-time differences as supporting asymmetric coupling and explicitly qualifies Pythia's uncertain multilingual suitability. It clarifies that POS templates cannot distinguish alternative parses sharing a tag sequence and expands the residual-information discussion toward functional, non-strictly linguistic knowledge.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly identifies residual-stream activations, and Appendix K supplies Pythia access and license information. Existing hardware, software, prompts and the code/data link remain. However, v1's statement promising a dataset release under CC BY 4.0 is removed.

R1.justification: v4 adds Biderman et al. on Pythia, Yin et al. concerning last-token representations, and Mahowald et al. on formal versus functional linguistic competence. These modestly extend positioning; the main related-work argument remains intact. The Shaib reference is an update to the same work.

P1.justification: v4 polishes wording, separates matched datasets from centroid construction, gives aggregation its own subsection, and moves the residual-norm discussion into the conclusion. Conference front matter and an impact statement are added, while most prose and the overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The ICML format substantially changes typography, captions and page layout, including single-column appendices. Existing appendix plots are enlarged and regrouped: v1 Figures 12 and 15 become separate figures in v4. Table 4's panels become side by side, and two new checkpoint figures are added.

improvement.justification: Corrected similarity and norm-decomposition formulas resolve concrete mathematical reporting errors, while checkpoint analyses and sensitivity checks strengthen support for the retained conclusions. The gains are limited by qualitative reporting of several checks and caveated Pythia multilingual suitability. Losing the explicit dataset licensing statement is a documentation drawback, but does not outweigh these improvements.
